tagline: A reconstructed fort and lock buildings tell two Kentucky River stories
intro: At Boonesborough, Kentucky Routes 388 and 627 meet beside a community on the Kentucky River. Fort Boonesborough State Park lies southeast of Lexington on the river’s west bank, with a reproduction fort containing cabins and bunkhouses.

In 1775, Richard Henderson hired Daniel Boone to cut a road into Kentucky for the Transylvania Company’s illegal colonial settlement attempt. Boone’s party included enslaved African Americans. After the Revolutionary War, Boonesborough became a stop for westward-bound settlers and a transit point for tobacco.

The local sequence runs from Boonesborough to the state park off Kentucky Route 627 and the Kentucky River Museum within it. The museum occupies the former Lock 10 operator’s home and its storage and maintenance building.

moments.title: Boonesborough
moments.text: Boonesborough served travelers heading farther into Kentucky, but it never attracted a substantial long-term population. Daniel Boone founded the settlement in 1775 while working for Richard Henderson and Nathanial Hart of the Transylvania Company. He lived here until 1779, then moved to his son Israel’s settlement near present-day Athens. The river settlement gradually declined; by 1877 it had almost disappeared as a village. Boonesborough is now an unincorporated community at the junction of Kentucky Routes 388 and 627. The region was then part of Virginia, which chartered Boonesborough in October 1779.

moments.title: Fort Boonesborough State Park
moments.text: The fort’s cabins and bunkhouses belong to a reproduction, not the original fortifications. The original settlement was eventually abandoned. Archaeological investigations in the 1980s identified the fortifications, tobacco warehouse foundations and a Fort Ancient village site. Fort Ancient residents had lived here circa 1400, before European colonial settlement. Within the reproduction fort, resident blacksmiths and potters give demonstrations during the season. The Kentucky River Museum interprets the river’s effects on families and commerce. Those excavations also identified water springs and Boone’s initial station, distinct elements within the larger archaeological site.
moments.notice: The reproduction fort contains cabins, bunkhouses and furnishings.

moments.title: Kentucky River Museum
moments.text: Lock 10’s former operator’s home became part of the Kentucky River Museum, established in 2002. The museum also occupies the lock’s storage and maintenance building. Lock 10 belongs to a series of fourteen Kentucky River locks originally built by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. Exhibits address the locks and dams of the 1900s and the river’s influence on local families and commerce.
